a_rows_sample.anchor: The Bayesian formalism provides a complete mathematical foundation for KnowledgeOS's epistemic state, updating mechanism, confirmation theory, decision theory, and justification.
a_rows_sample.statement: The document's culminating 'complete formal system for KnowledgeOS': Sigma_t = {cr_t(P): P in L} as the epistemic state; Sigma_{t+1} = Sigma_t(.|E_t) (or Jeffrey Conditionalization for uncertain evidence) as the transition; confirmation as E confirms H iff Sigma_t(H|E) > Sigma_t(H); decision as a_t = argmax_A sum_i u(A&S_i)*Sigma_t(S_i|A) (EDT) or the CDT analogue; and the Three Lenses re-stated as Zero (regularity/confirmation-measures/Scott Axiom), Lord (Bayes's theorem/likelihood ratios), Sarathi (decision theory/Conditionalization). Final claim: 'These are now formally available to KnowledgeOS' -- asserted without independent derivation or proof of fit to the prior KnowledgeOS kernel formalizations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Lord(K_t,Z_t,G,H_t) -> Proposal. It does not own the epistemic frame. ... S_t(K_t,Z_t,G,H_t,Proposal) -> Decision. Proposal != Decision.
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives refined typed signatures for Lord (Lord(K_t,Z_t,G,H_t) -> Proposal, explicitly not owning the epistemic frame) and Sarathi (S_t(K_t,Z_t,G,H_t,Proposal) -> Decision), re-affirming Proposal != Decision as an important invariant, and situates both within a full epistemic control loop Observation -> Evidence -> Extraction -> Determination -> K_t -> {IdealState, Zero} -> Gap Delta_t -> Lord -> Proposal -> Sarathi -> Decision -> authorization -> Action -> new Observation -> K_{t+1}.

a_rows_sample.anchor: d* = argmax_d E[Delta G_t | investigate d]. ... a_t* = argmax_a E[epistemic improvement|a] / cost(a)
a_rows_sample.statement: Gives Lord a concrete dimension-discovery objective -- choose the new dimension d expected to most reduce the epistemic-gap vector, d*=argmax_d E[Delta-G_t | investigate d] -- and Sarathi a concrete cost-normalized action-selection objective a_t*=argmax_a E[epistemic improvement|a]/cost(a), framed as deriving the architecture from the mathematics rather than the reverse.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ZERO-01 — Where did the prior come from? ... ZERO-12 — Representation itself can be wrong. ... InferenceCorrectness can coexist with RepresentationError.
b_rows_sample.statement: Twelve Zero-Lens gaps (ZERO-01 prior origin unexplained; ZERO-02 probability needs semantic reference; ZERO-03 incomplete hypothesis space; ZERO-04 incomplete evidence coverage; ZERO-05 untraced likelihood model; ZERO-06 missing environment/context; ZERO-07 undefined utility/objective; ZERO-08 model-prediction vs explanation vs reality-claim; ZERO-09 missing model failure/challenge/retirement/replacement; ZERO-10 exact vs approximate inference; ZERO-11 epistemic validity vs computational feasibility; ZERO-12 representation error coexisting with inference correctness), each producing a candidate Kernel requirement or object.

b_rows_sample.anchor: HypothesisSpace MUST be explicit for material probabilistic assessments. ... P(H1) + P(H2) = 1 could be mathematically correct while excluding H3 which is actually true.
b_rows_sample.statement: ZERO-03 worked example: a mathematically valid two-hypothesis probability sum can hide an unconsidered true third hypothesis, motivating the invariant that HypothesisSpace must be explicit for material probabilistic assessments.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Three converging admission conditions. *Standing* ... *prerequisite presence* ... *context sufficiency*
b_rows_sample.statement: Three genuinely different admission-condition questions are converging across the corpus: standing (was this input allowed to participate, S1-F032), prerequisite presence (what happens when a prerequisite is missing, the Zero lens, answered by ⟨Z-1⟩), and context sufficiency (have we understood the whole relevant context, the Leonardo lens). The reviewer confirms these are genuinely distinct questions and the convergence claim is sound.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Subtractive-structural, statistical-residual, and absence-typology are **three different operations under one name.**
b_rows_sample.statement: X-005: the corpus itself records two incompatible definitions of 'the Zero lens' 90 minutes apart, neither citing the other -- 'remove prior structure, ask what can be recovered from the source alone' (subtractive/structural, 20260824-152415, S1-F034) versus 'what statistically persists after explaining away non-knowledge' (statistical residual, 20260824-154254). Neither matches the absence typology (not mentioned != absent; absent from enumeration != excluded; not represented != zero; unknown != false; classes: zero/absence/unrepresented/unknown/not-applicable/excluded/not-tested) the reviewer has been applying in every review in this register, supplied by its own standing instructions. Three different operations share one name; this does not invalidate any finding (the reviewer's own usage is well-specified and consistent) but is a naming defect. Update (S2-R-F034.2): the lens was additionally used undefined for ~17 hours before any written definition existed (S1-F013, S1-F016, S1-F021 reached Zero-derived conclusions first), so the full picture is: used undefined, then defined twice incompatibly within 90 minutes, then a third sense applied by this reviewer -- meaning 'the Zero lens shows...' is not a single claim anywhere in the corpus.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the corpus's most-used instrument was **used undefined for ~17 hours**, then **defined twice incompatibly within 90 minutes**
b_rows_sample.statement: The Zero lens was defined on 2026-08-24 at 15:24 while in continuous use since 2026-08-23 -- a ~17 hour lag -- meaning every Zero-lens conclusion recorded before that timestamp (S1-F013, S1-F016, S1-F021) used an undefined instrument; recorded by Session 1 as a caveat, not invalidation, and the reviewer concurs. Combined with a separately recovered miss (S1-F024), the full picture is worse than either finding alone: used undefined for ~17 hours, then defined twice incompatibly within 90 minutes (subtractive-structural at 15:24:15; statistical-residual at 15:42:54), and this review's own session applies a third sense (absence typology, per X-005).

b_rows_sample.anchor: `revok` scoring zero in v1.1 does **not** establish that revocation is absent from KnowledgeOS. ... Concluding `IMPLEMENT` from a grep would be exactly the *not mentioned → absent* conversion I have charged others with.
b_rows_sample.statement: The reviewer applies the Zero lens to its own result: a zero grep-count for 'revok*' in v1.1 does not establish that revocation is absent from KnowledgeOS, because Authority is 'held by the Authority context' -- a supporting context whose internals v1.1 describes but does not specify -- and temporal validity of a grant may legitimately live there. What is established is narrower: the core model cannot express revocation-aware temporal validity, and nothing verifiable says the supporting context does either. Concluding IMPLEMENT from the grep alone would repeat the 'not mentioned -> absent' error charged against other findings in this register. Verdict: IMPLEMENTATION QUESTION, not IMPLEMENT.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
class GitaKnowledgeOS:
    """Complete KnowledgeOS derived from Bhagavad-gītā Chapter 4."""
b_rows_sample.statement: An integrated GitaKnowledgeOS class composes all twelve verse-derived components (lineage, memory, intervention, reward, duty, attachment, dual_analyzer, wise_state, evidence_paths, benefit, learning, closure) alongside the existing Zero/Lord/Sarathi lenses, with an evolve(event) method implementing an eight-step pipeline: observe (Sanjaya) -> interpret (semantic) -> evaluate (Zero, detect_gaps) -> generate (Lord, generate_candidates) -> guide (Sarathi, recommend) -> act (Arjuna, conditional on closure.is_ready_to_act()) -> learn (apply learning.learn()) -> purify (apply learning.purify()). A semantic-extraction helper (_extract_semantics) pattern-matches on literal substring presence in observation content ('action', 'teacher'/'wisdom', 'offering'/'sacrifice') to route to different SemanticStructure types, falling back to a generic 'GeneralObservation' type otherwise.

b_rows_sample.anchor: *Absence must not silently become an epistemic state*. ⟦L⟧ ⟨Z-1⟩ says exactly this. **CONSISTENT**, reached independently; ninth angle on the absence family.
b_rows_sample.statement: S1-F038's claim 'absence must not silently become an epistemic state' is confirmed as already stated by existing law (<Z-1>), reached independently -- classified CONSISTENT rather than corroborating, per the register's own standing rule about not treating instruction-derived matches as corroboration. Called the ninth angle on the corpus's recurring absence family of findings. Verdict: DO NOT IMPLEMENT (already protected). Separately, the corpus's explicit refusal to store epistemic state as possible worlds (following Gardenfors) is confirmed as converging with a separate resolution of a 'Fagin thread' elsewhere in the corpus -- a matter of placement (where the refusal belongs), not of ontology (what possible worlds are).

Elaborates the earlier Zero/Lord/Sarathi/Transition division with explicit role definitions: Zero detects gaps/conflicts/boundaries; Lord expands the possibility space; Sarathi navigates/guides; Transition actually changes state. The earlier Sarathi formalization is given a full function signature: Sarathi(K_t, Z_t, L_t, I_t, Q_t, C_t) -> a_t, where a_t is the next epistemic action -- described as remarkably close to what is now called action selection/guidance, though the modern formal model deliberately avoids promoting the old lens vocabulary into architectural objects. Confirms the earlier KnowledgeOS-as-Epistemic-Sarathi formulation (rather than an answer engine) and its See != Guide != Decide principle, noting it later became compatible with the modern formal chain Evidence != Determination != Proposal != Decision != Authorization != Action.

type_signature.domain: K_t, Z_t, L_t, I_t, Q_t, C_t

b_rows_sample.anchor: The Bayesian formalism provides a complete mathematical foundation for KnowledgeOS's epistemic state, updating mechanism, confirmation theory, decision theory, and justification.
b_rows_sample.statement: The document's culminating 'complete formal system for KnowledgeOS': Sigma_t = {cr_t(P): P in L} as the epistemic state; Sigma_{t+1} = Sigma_t(.|E_t) (or Jeffrey Conditionalization for uncertain evidence) as the transition; confirmation as E confirms H iff Sigma_t(H|E) > Sigma_t(H); decision as a_t = argmax_A sum_i u(A&S_i)*Sigma_t(S_i|A) (EDT) or the CDT analogue; and the Three Lenses re-stated as Zero (regularity/confirmation-measures/Scott Axiom), Lord (Bayes's theorem/likelihood ratios), Sarathi (decision theory/Conditionalization). Final claim: 'These are now formally available to KnowledgeOS' -- asserted without independent derivation or proof of fit to the prior KnowledgeOS kernel formalizations.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 3 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: A useful abstraction does not automatically deserve primitive status. ... Before adding an entity to the ontology, ask what work it actually does that its underlying structure cannot already do.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extracts Merricks' central move (statues need not be admitted into fundamental ontology if there are things 'arranged statuewise') as a methodological warning for KnowledgeOS: a useful abstraction (Knowledge, Assertion, Proposition, Question, Answer, Topic, Fact, Truth, Knowledge State) does not automatically deserve primitive status; before adding an entity to the ontology, ask what work it does that its underlying structure cannot already do.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Test A — What does X explain? Test B — What causal/operational work does X perform? Test C — Is that work already performed by its constituents and relationships? Test D — If we eliminate X, can we reconstruct everything we need?
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes a four-test 'KnowledgeOS eliminativism test' for any candidate primitive X (what does X explain; what work does it perform; is that work already done by constituents/relationships; can everything be reconstructed if X is eliminated), yielding a decision diagram: if constituents+relations can do the work, X is a projection/derived object; if not, X is a candidate primitive -- proposed as a formal architecture-discovery technique.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Is Assertion itself fundamental, or is it merely a useful abstraction over more primitive relationships? ... Agent -asserts-> Proposition -applies-in-> Context ... Assertion is the relationship/event that binds these together.
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies the eliminativism test to Assertion (currently modeled as owning Proposition/Context/Agent/Time/Provenance/Epistemic history), asking whether Assertion is fundamental or merely the relationship/event binding a more primitive Agent-asserts->Proposition-applies-in->Context structure -- an object-centric KnowledgeAssertionRecord versus a relationship/event-centric Assertion Act (by Agent, at Time, in Context, under Authority, with Provenance) -- stating KnowledgeOS may ultimately need the event-centric formulation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: time belongs to relationships/events, not necessarily to a monolithic "knowledge object." ... AssertionActivity — assertedAt; Observation — observedAt; ValidityClaim — validDuring; Evaluation — evaluatedAt; Supersession — supersededAt.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the temporal-role-separation principle (assertedAt/observedAt/validFrom/effectiveAt/evaluatedAt/supersededAt must not collapse into one timestamp) with a philosophical grounding: time belongs to relationships/events (AssertionActivity, Observation, ValidityClaim, Evaluation, Supersession, each with its own timestamp) rather than to one monolithic knowledge object, said to be compatible with the project's provenance/event-sourcing direction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: There may be no canonical "Knowledge" while there are assertions, propositions, observations, documents, relationships, assessments, events, contexts arranged knowledge-wise. ... There may be no canonical "Knowledge State" while there is a configuration of assertions and relationships that supports a particular knowledge-state projection.
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies Merricks' 'arranged statuewise' move directly: there may be no canonical 'Knowledge' object, only assertions/propositions/observations/documents/relationships/assessments/events/contexts arranged 'knowledge-wise'; likewise no canonical 'Knowledge State' object, only a configuration of assertions and relationships supporting a knowledge-state projection -- called a huge conceptual simplification, and offered as the solution to the recurring 'what is the current state of knowledge?' problem: current knowledge is a projection, not an object in the ontology.

a_rows_sample.anchor: FALSE ≠ UNFOUNDED ≠ USELESS ... a false belief about a statue can nevertheless be grounded by there being things arranged statuewise. ... KnowledgeOS therefore should preserve: semantic status + structural grounding + practical adequacy rather than merely truth = false.
a_rows_sample.statement: Uses Merricks' 'nearly as good as true' idea (a false folk belief about a statue can still be grounded by an underlying statuewise arrangement) to derive FALSE != UNFOUNDED != USELESS: e.g. 'the service is a Kafka service' might be semantically wrong under strict ontology yet be a highly useful approximation given observed configuration/Kafka dependency/topics/runtime traffic, so KnowledgeOS should preserve semantic status + structural grounding + practical adequacy rather than collapsing to truth=false; connects to the earlier conclusion that assessment is an act, not an intrinsic property.

a_rows_sample.anchor: STRUCTURAL GROUNDING: directly grounded, approximately grounded, arrangement-supported, convention-supported, projection-derived, unsupported. ... An assertion can be false while still being strongly grounded in the underlying structure. That is very different from hallucination.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a new Structural Grounding dimension (directly grounded / approximately grounded / arrangement-supported / convention-supported / projection-derived / unsupported) alongside existing epistemic status (asserted/supported/verified/disputed/superseded), asserting an assertion can be false while strongly grounded in underlying structure -- explicitly distinguished from hallucination, illustrated by contrasting a Kafka-service claim (strong evidence, strong structural correspondence, possibly still 'wrong') against 'the service uses magical quantum middleware' (unsupported assertion, no evidence, no structural correspondence) -- both potentially false but epistemically very different, called exactly the distinction an AI engineering knowledge system needs.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ordinary language doesn't necessarily reveal fundamental ontology. ... "Knowledge says..." "Architecture knows..." "The system understands..." ... Natural-language grammar must not determine domain ontology.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extracts Merricks' argument that ordinary-language statue-talk does not reveal fundamental ontology, applying it to LLM output: grammatical constructions like 'Knowledge says...', 'Architecture knows...', 'The system understands...', 'The document proves...', 'The model believes...' can hide radically different underlying structures, yielding the major architectural rule: natural-language grammar must not determine domain ontology.

a_rows_sample.anchor: "The authentication service uses Redis." We should NOT automatically create: Knowledge -> fact -> service uses Redis. Instead: Representation -> Semantic interpretation -> Proposition -> Assertion candidate -> Evidence -> Assessment. The language output is merely the surface representation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies the natural-language-grammar warning specifically to LLM-generated claims: an LLM statement ('the authentication service uses Redis') must not be auto-promoted to Knowledge->fact, but must pass through Representation->Semantic interpretation->Proposition->Assertion candidate (source/context/time/provenance)->Evidence->Assessment, reinforcing the model developed across S0505-S0510.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Don't create a giant aggregate merely because several objects participate in one conceptual structure. ... These may form a knowledge graph/reconstruction graph, but that does not mean they belong inside one transactional aggregate. ... Preservation unit ≠ Aggregate ≠ Knowledge graph ≠ Projection.
a_rows_sample.statement: Uses Merricks' rejection of composition-as-identity (a whole is not simply identical to its many parts) to warn against a giant 'KnowledgeAggregate' containing Assertion/Proposition/Evidence/Observation/Document/Question/Assessment/Agent/Context merely because they participate in one conceptual structure -- they may form a knowledge graph/reconstruction graph without belonging inside one transactional aggregate, reinforcing preservation unit != aggregate != knowledge graph != projection.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Non-Redundant Work Principle: A KnowledgeOS concept should become a Kernel primitive only when it performs non-redundant preservation, consistency, identity, or reconstruction work that cannot be adequately provided by its constituent entities, relationships, events, and policies. ... Does Assertion have non-redundant work? ... identify / challenge / supersede / evaluate / preserve its epistemic history.
a_rows_sample.statement: Names the file's central architecture heuristic, the 'Non-Redundant Work Principle': a KnowledgeOS concept becomes a Kernel primitive only when it performs non-redundant preservation/consistency/identity/reconstruction work that its constituent entities/relationships/events/policies cannot adequately provide; applies it as a test to Assertion (can we identify/challenge/supersede/evaluate it, preserve its epistemic history?) -- if these operations genuinely require an identity-bearing assertion, Assertion deserves first-class status; if reducible to Proposition+Agent+Context+Event, it is a derived construct -- explicitly stating this has not yet been proven either way.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A projection can be operationally valid without being ontologically fundamental. ... Current Architecture, Current Knowledge, Topic, Summary, Answer, Recommendation, Risk Score, Knowledge Graph ... may all be extremely useful. But they don't therefore belong in the Kernel. ... the cleanest answer we've found to the question: "What is KnowledgeOS versus what KnowledgeOS produces?"
a_rows_sample.statement: States a second principle, separating metaphysical truth from practical usefulness per Merricks (everyday statue-talk remains useful even under eliminativism): 'a projection can be operationally valid without being ontologically fundamental', illustrated by Current Architecture, Current Knowledge, Topic, Summary, Answer, Recommendation, Risk Score, and Knowledge Graph all being useful without belonging in the Kernel, described as the cleanest answer found yet to 'what is KnowledgeOS versus what KnowledgeOS produces?'

a_rows_sample.anchor: FUNDAMENTAL PRESERVED STRUCTURE (Identity, Context, Provenance, Proposition, Assertion, Temporal with Evidence/Assessment/Challenge/Supersession) versus DERIVED/PROJECTED VIEWS (Topic, Current State, Answer) ... even this diagram should remain a hypothesis.
a_rows_sample.statement: Redraws the Knowledge Space as splitting into Fundamental Preserved Structure (Identity, Context, Provenance, Proposition, Assertion with Temporal/Evidence/Assessment/Challenge/Supersession sub-relations) versus Derived/Projected Views (Topic, Current State, Answer), explicitly labeling even this diagram a hypothesis, not a decided ontology, per Merricks' warning against premature ontology promotion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What entities and relationships must exist in the KnowledgeOS Kernel such that every useful higher-level knowledge construct can be reconstructed without loss? ... Is Assertion genuinely a non-redundant KnowledgeOS primitive, or is it itself a useful higher-level object emerging from more fundamental assertion-events, propositions, contexts, agents and relations? I would not freeze the Assertion Aggregate until we answer that question.
a_rows_sample.statement: Sharpens the Kernel question from 'what is the smallest thing KnowledgeOS must preserve?' (answered: an identity-bearing assertion relationship, S0510) to 'what entities and relationships must exist in the Kernel such that every useful higher-level knowledge construct can be reconstructed without loss?', summarizing Merricks' method as a seven-step discipline (start with ordinary conceptual objects -> ask what underlying structure makes them useful -> remove the candidate -> see what capabilities disappear -> nothing essential disappears = projection/abstraction -> non-redundant work disappears = candidate primitive -> preserve the underlying structure even when eliminating the higher-level object), and explicitly declines to freeze the Assertion Aggregate until the open question (is Assertion genuinely non-redundant?) is answered.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A thing deserves fundamental status when removing it causes the loss of some non-redundant capability that cannot be reconstructed from the remaining structure. ... Merricks himself does not give us a numerical metric for "non-redundant causal power."
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates the Non-Redundant Work Principle as a candidate ontological criterion, explicitly noting it remains qualitative since Merricks provides no numerical metric for non-redundant causal power, motivating the file's quantification effort.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Identity Necessity — I ... 0 = no independent identity ... 5 = impossible to reconstruct without identity. ... Non-Redundant Work — N ... What operation becomes impossible or materially ambiguous if this object disappears? ... This is the most important metric.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Identity Necessity I (a 0-5 scale for whether a concept needs its own stable identity, e.g. Assertion scoring high, Knowledge Summary scoring low) and Non-Redundant Work N (the Merricks-inspired metric: what operation becomes impossible or materially ambiguous if the object disappears -- e.g. Assertion's challenge/supersede/assess/trace/reconstruct operations versus KnowledgeSummary merely regrouping existing information), calling N the most important metric.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Reconstruction Loss — R ... R = proportion of required capabilities lost ... Topic: 100% | Summary: 100% | Current Knowledge State: 95% | Assertion: maybe 40-70% | Proposition: maybe 30-60% | Evidence: potentially very high. The numbers are not known yet.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Reconstruction Loss R as the proportion of required capabilities lost after removing a candidate and attempting downstream reconstruction, with a speculative worked table (Topic 100%, Summary 100%, Current Knowledge State 95%, Assertion maybe 40-70%, Proposition maybe 30-60%, Evidence potentially very high), explicitly flagged as unknown values to be experimentally determined, not settled figures.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Temporal Irreducibility — T ... Provenance Irreducibility — P ... Governance/Transaction Necessity — G — This is the dimension Merricks doesn't give us, but KnowledgeOS absolutely needs it. ... Does this concept have to be independently governed, versioned, challenged, authorized, preserved, or committed?
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Temporal Irreducibility T (can temporal history -- who asserted P, when, under which context/version/assessment/supersession -- be reconstructed without the candidate?), Provenance Irreducibility P (can provenance -- source/observation/agent/time/assessment chain -- be reconstructed without it?), and Governance/Transaction Necessity G (must the concept be independently governed/versioned/challenged/authorized/preserved/committed, e.g. Assertion vs Topic used only for navigation), explicitly noting G is a dimension Merricks' philosophy does not supply but KnowledgeOS requires.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K(X) = w_I I(X) + w_N N(X) + w_R R(X) + w_T T(X) + w_P P(X) + w_G G(X) ... We don't need to choose the weights yet. In fact, choosing weights too early would be a mistake.
a_rows_sample.statement: Combines the five dimensions into a weighted Kernel-candidacy score K(X)=w_I*I(X)+w_N*N(X)+w_R*R(X)+w_T*T(X)+w_P*P(X)+w_G*G(X), each dimension normalized to [0,1], with an explicit warning against choosing weights before collecting evidence.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Projection Equivalence — E ... Can X be generated deterministically from lower-level primitives? ... CurrentKnowledgeState = projection(assertions, assessments, temporal rules, authority rules) ... D(X) = degree to which X is deterministically derivable ... K(X) ∝ 1-D(X).
a_rows_sample.statement: Adds a seventh dimension, Projection Equivalence/derivability D(X): if X=f(A,B,C,D) for a deterministic, lossless f (e.g. CurrentKnowledgeState=projection(assertions,assessments,temporal rules,authority rules)), X is probably derived, not Kernel; formalizes K(X) proportional to 1-D(X).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Persons and objects are not merely two kinds of "things." Persons introduce agency, reasons, intentions, and causal powers into the space. Causes introduce directed dependency between things, states, events, and actions. ... Cause -> RELATION / DEPENDENCY
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects a model that would treat Person, Object, and Cause as equivalent node types: Person and Object are both entities/nodes but Person additionally carries agency, beliefs, desires, reasons, intentions, and action-capacity beyond Object's mere properties/capacities; Cause is not an entity at all but a relation/dependency type (e.g. Fire--causes-->heating, Person--causes-->intention), citing O'Connor's distinction between event causation and agent causation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: particulars have properties → properties ground causal capacities → capacities can be exercised → effects occur. ... capacity / capacity becomes an important bridge between WHAT SOMETHING IS and WHAT SOMETHING CAN DO.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes O'Connor's causal-capacity structure for objects (Object->Properties->Causal capacity->[circumstances]->Effect) and agents (Person->{beliefs,desires,reasons}->Agent capacity->Intention->Action), illustrated by 'a person can open the door' requiring bodily capability+knowledge+desire+opportunity before capacity-to-act yields possible action; Capacity is identified as the bridge concept between what something is and what it can do.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Person -> believes X, desires Y, has reason R -> deliberation -> intention -> action ... KnowledgeOS can represent not just: what happened? but: why did it happen? That is a completely different class of knowledge.
b_rows_sample.statement: Chains reasons/beliefs/desires into a deliberation->intention->action sequence, arguing this lets KnowledgeOS represent 'why did it happen' as a distinct knowledge class from 'what happened', citing O'Connor's connection of actions to the agent's desire-belief complexes or reasons.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS doesn't necessarily need a primitive object called Knowledge. Instead it can represent: PERSON Alice, EVENT opening-the-door, ... REASON wanting-to-leave, CAUSAL/EXPLANATORY RELATION wanting-to-leave --explains--> opening-the-door, TRUTH-BEARER ... The knowledge emerges from the structured configuration.
b_rows_sample.statement: Decomposes 'Alice opened the door because she wanted to leave' into Person/Event/Object/Mental-State/Reason/Causal-Explanatory-Relation/Truth-bearer/Truth-status/Evidence/Source without any primitive 'Knowledge' object, concluding knowledge emerges from the structured configuration -- explicitly connected to Merricks' 'arranged-X-wise' eliminativism.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Cause ≠ explanation, Person ≠ object, Reason ≠ cause, Action ≠ event-description, Capacity ≠ actual exercise. ... Knowledge is not a primitive bucket containing facts. Knowledge is structured intelligibility over different kinds of entities, states, events, relations, reasons, causes, and truth-bearers.
b_rows_sample.statement: Combines Merricks' non-collapses (Truth≠evidence≠aboutness≠truthmaker) with five new O'Connor-derived non-collapses (Cause≠explanation, Person≠object, Reason≠cause, Action≠event-description, Capacity≠actual exercise) into the central converging principle: knowledge is not a primitive bucket containing facts, but structured intelligibility over different kinds of entities, states, events, relations, reasons, causes, and truth-bearers.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Dimension A — What exists / what we refer to (Particulars: Objects/Persons-Agents/Events/States/Situations; Universals/Properties: Properties/Capacities/Powers/Relations) ... Dimension B — How things are connected (identity, instantiation, part-of, about, causes, enables, prevents, depends-on, explains, supports, intends, believes, desires, acts-on) ... Knowledge Space = Entities × Relations × States × Claims × Contexts.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes two intersecting dimensions for the Knowledge Space instead of one hierarchy: Dimension A (particulars: objects/persons/events/states/situations vs universals: properties/capacities/powers/relations, citing O'Connor's particular/universal distinction) and Dimension B (fourteen relation types: identity, instantiation, part-of, about, causes, enables, prevents, depends-on, explains, supports, intends, believes, desires, acts-on), combined as Knowledge Space = Entities x Relations x States x Claims x Contexts.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Persons are not merely objects inside Knowledge Space. They are participants that traverse and transform Knowledge Space. ... a person is simultaneously an entity + a bearer of properties + a causal agent + a source of reasons + a holder of beliefs + a holder of intentions + an actor + an observer + a knower + a producer of claims.
b_rows_sample.statement: Identifies Person as the bridge between ontology and epistemology, being simultaneously entity, bearer-of-properties, causal agent, source of reasons, holder of beliefs/intentions, actor, observer, knower, and producer of claims, so that WORLD->perception->PERSON->{belief,reasoning,intention,decision,action}->WORLD; concludes persons are participants that traverse and transform Knowledge Space, not merely objects inside it. (This claim is explicitly challenged as architectural 'overreach' later in this same file's Critical Analysis section.)

b_rows_sample.anchor: humans don't merely ask: What caused X? They ask: Why X? Those aren't always identical. ... KnowledgeOS probably needs CAUSE and separately EXPLANATION, with relationships between them ... physical explanation, causal explanation, functional explanation, intentional explanation, reasons explanation, historical explanation, logical explanation ... without pretending they're all the same thing.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes CAUSE from EXPLANATION as separate KnowledgeOS concepts with relationships between them, since 'why X?' is not always identical to 'what caused X?', enumerating seven non-identical explanation kinds (physical, causal, functional, intentional, reasons, historical, logical) that must not be treated as the same thing, citing O'Connor's exploration of the relationship between causal and reasons-based explanation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge Space is not primarily a hierarchy of topics. It is a relational space whose nodes represent entities, events, states, properties, propositions and mental contents, while its edges represent relations such as identity, instantiation, aboutness, causation, explanation, dependence, support, intention and agency. Then topics become views over that space. Not primitives.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the file's central research hypothesis: Knowledge Space is a relational space (nodes: entities/events/states/properties/propositions/mental contents; edges: identity/instantiation/aboutness/causation/explanation/dependence/support/intention/agency), not a hierarchy of topics; Topics become projections over this space rather than primitives, illustrated by 'Topic: Free Will' as a projection over Persons+Actions+Reasons+Intentions+Causes+Possibilities+Responsibility+Time+Truth-claims.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Merricks: Truth cannot be reduced to truthmaking/evidence/aboutness. O'Connor: Persons, objects, properties, powers, causes, reasons, intentions and actions cannot simply be collapsed into events or objects. Our KnowledgeOS investigation: Knowledge must remain reconstructible, contextual, governed and evidentially traceable. ... Is this a primitive entity, a relation, a property, a state, a representation, a perspective, or merely a useful projection?
b_rows_sample.statement: States three converging constraints from Merricks, O'Connor, and the project's own KnowledgeOS investigation, concluding the right next step is not to declare an ontology but to run a 'Knowledge Space Ontological Discovery' over 22 candidates (Persons, Objects, Properties, Events, States, Actions, Agents, Causes, Effects, Powers, Capacities, Reasons, Intentions, Claims, Propositions, Truth, Evidence, Sources, Contexts, Time, Modality, Explanation), asking of each whether it is a primitive entity, relation, property, state, representation, perspective, or merely a useful projection.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The Kernel should preserve records of agency (who asserted what, based on what reasons), not implement agency itself. ... KnowledgeOS cannot be the arbiter of what truly explains what. That would be a semantic oracle. ... The correct response is: The Kernel should preserve claims about explanation, not the explanations themselves.
b_rows_sample.statement: Warns against four dangers of importing O'Connor's framework uncritically: (1) treating Person/Agent Causation/Intention/Action as Kernel primitives would make the Kernel a metaphysical engine -- the Kernel should preserve records of agency, not implement agency; (2) the Kernel becoming an arbiter of what truly causes/explains what would make it a 'semantic oracle' -- it should preserve claims about explanation, not the explanations themselves (paralleling Assertion-preserved vs Truth-evaluated-externally); (3) capacities/powers are notoriously hard to formalize (counterfactuals, contexts, degrees, interactions) and belong in assertion content, not Kernel structure; (4) treating persons as active Kernel-level transformers of Knowledge Space is overreach -- the Kernel should preserve records of participation (who made what claim, when, based on what), not model transformative agency itself.

b_rows_sample.anchor: McGinn (Logical): Identity, Existence, Predication, Necessity, Truth. O'Connor (Metaphysical): Persons, Objects, Properties, Powers/Capacities, Causes, Reasons, Intentions, Actions. ... The Kernel should preserve McGinn's logical properties. ... The Kernel should NOT implement O'Connor's metaphysical categories. They are the content of knowledge claims.
b_rows_sample.statement: Cross-checks O'Connor's metaphysical categories against McGinn's logical properties, concluding the Kernel preserves McGinn's five logical properties (invariant structure of any knowledge claim) and must not implement O'Connor's metaphysical categories (which are the semantic content of knowledge claims, not Kernel structure), giving a three-level architecture: Kernel Level (Identity/Existence/Predication/Necessity/Truth), Content Level (Persons/Objects/Properties/Powers-Capacities/Causes/Reasons/Intentions/Actions, each 'as claimed'/'as asserted', never as Kernel primitives), and Explanation Level bridge (Explanation Records: causal/reasons/intentional/explanatory claims, preserved as content).

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeAssertionRecord ... relationRefs: CAUSAL_CLAIM: (WANTING-TO-LEAVE → OPENING-DOOR); EXPLANATORY_CLAIM ...; AGENT_CLAIM ...; REASON_CLAIM ... ... The Kernel should NOT: Determine whether Alice actually wanted to leave; Determine whether the desire caused the action; Determine whether the explanation is true; Model "agent causation" as a Kernel primitive.
b_rows_sample.statement: Provides a fully worked test case ('Alice opened the door because she wanted to leave') showing exactly what the Kernel preserves -- a KnowledgeAssertionRecord (id, propositionRef, contextRef, assertedBy, assertedAt, temporalScope, epistemicCommitment, relationRefs including CAUSAL_CLAIM, EXPLANATORY_CLAIM, AGENT_CLAIM, REASON_CLAIM) -- against a six-item list of what the Kernel must never do (determine whether Alice actually wanted to leave, whether the desire caused the action, whether the explanation is true, model agent causation or capacity as primitives, or treat person differently from object at the Kernel level), with those determinations explicitly assigned to outside Semantic Interpretation, Evaluation, and Reasoning layers.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The Space Is Not Flat ... nine distinct ontological regions ... Relations Are Not Uniform ... nine distinct relation types ... The Space Has Directionality ... TEMPORAL: Past → Present → Future ... EXPLANATORY: Cause → Effect (causal); Reason → Action (intentional); Ground → Claim (epistemic); Premise → Conclusion (logical).
b_rows_sample.statement: Summarizes three structural discoveries about the Knowledge Space: it has nine distinct ontological regions (Objects, Persons, Events, States, Properties, Powers/Capacities, Causes, Reasons, Explanations); relations are not uniform, spanning nine distinct types (Identity, Instantiation, Causation, Agent Causation, Explanation, Intention, Belief, Desire, Representation); and the space has directionality both temporal (Past->Present->Future) and explanatory (Cause->Effect causal; Reason->Action intentional; Ground->Claim epistemic; Premise->Conclusion logical), each direction type kept distinct.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The Persons and Causes Lens ... Is this entity an object with causal powers, or a person with reasons, intentions, and agency? ... Knowledge is not just about facts. It's about persons, reasons, intentions, actions, causes, and explanations. ... Reason ≠ Cause (Persons and Causes lens); Person ≠ Object (Persons and Causes lens); Explanation ≠ Event (Persons and Causes lens).
b_rows_sample.statement: Names 'the Persons and Causes Lens' with defining question 'is this entity an object with causal powers, or a person with reasons, intentions, and agency?', usable as adversarial lens/content specification/boundary warning; closes with the bottom line that knowledge is about persons, reasons, intentions, actions, causes and explanations (expanding what must be preservable) without the Kernel needing to implement agency, causation, explanation, or intentionality, extending the project's non-collapse family (Expression≠Meaning, Truth≠Proof, Assertion≠Reality) with Reason≠Cause, Person≠Object, Explanation≠Event.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Layer 0 — Logical primitives: Identity, Predication, Existence, Truth, Necessity/Modality ... These are not ordinary knowledge objects. They define the space in which knowledge can be represented. ... Layer 1 — Ontological particulars ... Layer 2 — Properties and powers ... Layer 3 — Relations ... Layer 4 — Epistemic representations ... Truth is not merely another epistemic attribute. It connects the epistemic representation back toward reality.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a five-layer KnowledgeOS architecture: Layer 0 Logical primitives (Identity, Predication, Existence, Truth, Necessity/Modality -- defining the representational space itself, not ordinary knowledge objects); Layer 1 Ontological particulars (Person, Object, Event, State, Situation); Layer 2 Properties and powers (Property, Capacity, Causal Power, Disposition, Role, State); Layer 3 Relations (identity, instantiation, part-of, causes, enables, depends-on, supports, explains, intends, believes); Layer 4 Epistemic representations (Claim, Proposition, Observation, Evidence, Source, Argument, Inference, Interpretation), with Truth singled out as connecting the epistemic representation back toward reality rather than being merely another epistemic attribute.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Persons and Causes gave us the dynamics of the space. Logical Properties gives us the structural grammar of the space. ... KnowledgeOS is fundamentally a structured space of predication and reference over entities, properties, events and agents, constrained by identity, existence, truth and modality, with causal, explanatory, evidential and intentional relations connecting the structures.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the file's converging hypothesis combining both McGinn and O'Connor readings: KnowledgeOS is fundamentally a structured space of predication and reference over entities, properties, events and agents, constrained by identity, existence, truth and modality, with causal, explanatory, evidential and intentional relations connecting the structures -- explicitly held as a hypothesis not yet implemented.

b_rows_sample.anchor: current knowledge includes C and E -> temporarily remove C -> ask whether E becomes less expected -> C has causal relevance. His probabilistic criterion is that, in the contracted epistemic state, occurrence of C raises the probability of E. ... probabilistic influence alone does not automatically establish causation ... P(E|C) > P(E) is not automatically C causes E. ... preserve causal_hypothesis separately from statistical_association.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes causal belief via contraction: temporarily remove candidate cause C from the epistemic state and test whether effect E becomes less expected (probabilistic criterion: in the contracted state, C's occurrence raises P(E)); connects this to the project's Persons+Causes research, proposing KnowledgeOS distinguish observed sequence/correlation/causal belief/causal evidence/causal hypothesis/causal explanation; explicitly warns P(E|C)>P(E) does not automatically establish C causes E (spurious/direct/indirect causes need additional treatment), requiring causal_hypothesis be preserved separately from statistical_association.

b_rows_sample.anchor: # 7. This connects directly to our "Persons and Causes" work
b_rows_sample.statement: Connects Searle's institutional layer to the earlier O'Connor Persons and Causes work by distinguishing natural/physical capacity from institutional power, and introduces 'deontic power' (rights, obligations, duties, privileges, permissions, requirements, authorizations, entitlements) as the content that institutional status can generate.

a_rows_sample.anchor: if we simply introduce an "ontology" into KnowledgeOS, it can become a giant taxonomy that tries to define the meaning of everything. ... KnowledgeOS does not own all meaning. It owns the semantic mechanisms by which meanings are declared, scoped, related, compared, and governed.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the governing principle 'KnowledgeOS does not own all meaning' — it owns only the semantic mechanisms by which meanings are declared, scoped, related, compared, and governed, rejecting a giant universal ontology.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The fundamental problem ... "Backup" ... a copy of data ... the backup execution process ... a business continuity capability ... a database backup artifact ... a contractual obligation. Word\neq Concept. Same word\neq Same meaning.
a_rows_sample.statement: Illustrates with five different meanings of 'Backup' that Word ≠ Concept and Same word ≠ Same meaning.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Lexical identity versus conceptual identity ... "Backup" is a lexical expression. But DatabaseBackup, BackupExecution, BackupArtifact, BusinessContinuityBackup may be different concepts. LexicalIdentity\neq ConceptualIdentity. This prevents one of the most dangerous failures in an enterprise knowled
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Lexeme from Concept — LexicalIdentity ≠ ConceptualIdentity — explicitly to prevent 'semantic false merging', named as one of the most dangerous enterprise knowledge-graph failures.

a_rows_sample.anchor: What is a Concept? ... Concept=(ConceptID,Meaning,Context,Constraints,Relations,Terminology) ... The crucial field is Context.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Concept=(ConceptID,Meaning,Context,Constraints,Relations,Terminology), flagging Context as the crucial field.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Concept meaning is contextual ... Meaning(c,C) ... Meaning(c,C_1) may differ from Meaning(c,C_2). This is exactly what DDD bounded contexts formalize. ... Bounded Context ... BC=(Concepts,Terms,Rules,Relationships,Context) ... Sales Context: Customer = contracting organization ... Identity Context:
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines context-relative Meaning(c,C) and a Bounded Context BC=(Concepts,Terms,Rules,Relationships,Context), worked with a three-context 'Customer' example showing Term(Customer,BC1)≠Term(Customer,BC2).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Same concept, different terms ... "Employee" "Staff Member" "Personnel" may refer to the same conceptual entity. Different terms \not\Rightarrow Different concepts. We therefore need semantic equivalence explicitly represented.
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows the reverse case — Employee/Staff Member/Personnel as one concept — establishing Different terms ⇏ Different concepts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Ubiquitous Language ... The language of a bounded context defines Term\rightarrow Concept. "ElectionCommittee" \rightarrow Concept:C_{EC} within ElectionManagement. KnowledgeOS should preserve that mapping rather than inventing its own universal meaning.
a_rows_sample.statement: Adopts DDD's Ubiquitous Language mechanism (Term→Concept mapping owned by a bounded context) rather than KnowledgeOS inventing its own universal meaning.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Semantic assertion ... "Backup means a copy of recoverable data." is itself an assertion. SemanticDefinition\in KnowledgeState. It has evidence; provenance; validity; context; epistemic status. This is important because even definitions can change.
a_rows_sample.statement: States a semantic definition is itself a KnowledgeState assertion (with evidence/provenance/validity/context/epistemic status), since even definitions can change.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Ontology versus knowledge ... Ontology What kinds of concepts and relationships exist ... Knowledge What is currently believed/accepted about particular instances. BackupArtifact subtypeOf DataArtifact. BackupArtifact(B_123). Ontology\neq InstanceKnowledge. ... Ontology as a model ... \mathcal O=(C,
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Ontology (conceptual model, e.g. subtype axioms) from InstanceKnowledge (concrete instances), formalized as O=(C,R,A,K) — concepts, relations, axioms, terminology mappings.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Not every relationship is the same ... A\rightarrow B ... is-a; part-of; depends-on; causes; precedes; implements; contradicts; supports; derived-from; governed-by. RelationshipType is semantically significant. We cannot use an undifferentiated graph edge. ... Typed relations ... r=(Source,Type,Targ
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues an untyped graph edge is insufficient given ten different possible relationship semantics, defining typed relations r=(Source,Type,Target,Context,Constraints).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Relation epistemology ... r = (Source,Type,Target,\Sigma,Evidence,Provenance,TemporalScope). This means we can say: We believe that Nexus depends on this firewall rule. without claiming that the dependency is an absolute truth.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends typed relations with epistemic fields (Σ,Evidence,Provenance,TemporalScope) so a relation can be believed without claiming absolute truth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Ontological axioms ... Employee\subseteq Person ... EveryElection\rightarrow hasCommittee ... ElectionCommittee\subseteq OrganizationUnit. These are not ordinary observations. They are SemanticRules/Axioms. Their provenance must be explicit. ... Three different sources of semantics ... Domain expert
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes ontological axioms (SemanticRules/Axioms, requiring explicit provenance) from ordinary observations, and classifies four distinct sources of semantics (domain experts, standards/textbooks, organizational governance, derived inference) that must not be treated identically.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Constitution versus ontology ... All production changes require approval. ... ProductionChange subtypeOf Change. Ontology answers: What is this thing? Constitution answers: What must or must not happen? Semantics\neq Governance. ... Ontology versus policy ... Migration is a Change. versus Migration\
a_rows_sample.statement: Draws a core invariant separating descriptive semantics (Ontology: 'what is this thing?') from normative rules (Constitution/Policy: 'what must happen?') — Semantics≠Governance, DescriptiveSemantics≠NormativeRules.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Concepts, assertions, and rules ... Concept C What something means. Assertion A What is claimed about something. Rule R What follows or must happen under specified conditions. Concept: Backup. Assertion: Backup(B_123). Rule: ProductionSystem \land CriticalBackup \Rightarrow RestoreTestRequired.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes three layers — Concept (meaning), Assertion (claim), Rule (conditional consequence) — worked with a Backup/Backup(B123)/RestoreTestRequired example.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The semantic universe ... \mathcal M=(\mathcal C,\mathcal R,\mathcal A,\mathcal P,\mathcal G) ... concepts; typed relations; axioms; predicates/rules; governance semantics. But I would not put all of these into one monolithic ontology. They should remain distinct bounded concerns.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the semantic universe M=(Concepts,Relations,Axioms,Predicates/Rules,GovernanceSemantics) while explicitly refusing to unify them into one monolithic ontology.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Semantic context ... Every concept should carry ContextID ... ConceptID + ContextID determines its contextual identity. This avoids the dangerous assumption: GlobalConceptMeaning.
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires every concept carry a ContextID so ConceptID+ContextID (not ConceptID alone) determines contextual identity, avoiding a dangerous assumption of GlobalConceptMeaning.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Cross-context mapping ... C_1=Customer_{Sales} and C_2=Customer_{Billing}. C_1 mapsTo C_2. But mapping does not necessarily mean equality. Possible mappings include Equivalent, BroaderThan, NarrowerThan, RelatedTo, TranslatesTo, PartiallyCorrespondsTo. ... Semantic alignment ... Alignment(C_1,C_2,M)
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines cross-context mapping via six mapping types (Equivalent/BroaderThan/NarrowerThan/RelatedTo/TranslatesTo/PartiallyCorrespondsTo), formalized as an epistemic Alignment(C1,C2,M) object with its own Support level.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Semantic equivalence is not automatic ... "Application" and "System" ... KnowledgeOS must not automatically infer Application=System. It may propose CandidateEquivalent. Then evidence and context determine whether the mapping is accepted. SemanticSimilarity\neq SemanticIdentity. ... LLMs and semanti
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns against automatically inferring semantic identity from apparent similarity (Application vs System) — SemanticSimilarity ≠ SemanticIdentity — with LLM-proposed mappings entering only as CandidateSemanticMapping, governed by the kernel: 'LLM proposes; KnowledgeOS governs.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Concept identity ... C_{472} might represent Nexus Repository Manager instance. Its terms could be Nexus, Nexus Repository, Repository Manager, Nexus OSS within different contexts. The identity remains ConceptID=C_{472}. ... Entity versus concept ... Concept A class/category. Entity A concrete insta
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a stable ConceptID independent of surface terminology, and distinguishes Concept (class/category) from Entity (concrete instance) — Concept ≠ Entity, connecting to the Step 12 identity model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Entity membership ... InstanceOf(Nexus_{DGNEX},NexusRepositoryManager). This is a semantic relation. But again, the membership itself has epistemic status. Support=Strong. ... Contextual identity of entities ... Infrastructure Context: NexusServer ... Application Context: RepositoryService ... Secur
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines InstanceOf membership as an epistemically-governed semantic relation, and shows the same underlying entity can have context-specific representations (Infrastructure/Application/Security views), requiring IdentityResolution across contexts.

b_rows_sample.anchor: When KnowledgeOS derives something, what exactly gives it the right to derive it? ... A mathematical theorem, a business policy, a causal hypothesis, an architectural constraint, a statistical model, and an LLM suggestion may all look like rules, but they have completely different epistemic and oper
b_rows_sample.statement: States the governing principle of Step 18: Rule ≠ Inference ≠ Truth ≠ Policy, since mathematical theorems, business policies, causal hypotheses, architectural constraints, statistical models, and LLM suggestions all superficially look like rules but carry completely different epistemic meanings.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The fundamental problem ... A\Rightarrow B ... Logical implication A\vdash B ... Mathematical theorem A\models B ... Business rule ... Architectural constraint ... Causal claim A\rightarrow_c B ... Statistical relationship P(B\mid A)>P(B) ... Heuristic ... LLM-generated hypothesis ... These are fund
b_rows_sample.statement: Shows a single arrow notation A⇒B could denote eight fundamentally different things (logical implication, mathematical theorem, business rule, architectural constraint, causal claim, statistical relationship, heuristic, LLM hypothesis), requiring KnowledgeOS to adopt typed inference semantics.

b_rows_sample.anchor: What is a Rule? ... R=(RuleID,Kind,Premises,Conclusion,Semantics,Context,Authority,Validity,Version,Provenance). The most important addition is Kind.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Rule=(RuleID,Kind,Premises,Conclusion,Semantics,Context,Authority,Validity,Version,Provenance), flagging Kind as the most important addition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Rule kinds ... \mathcal R=\{Logical,Mathematical,Semantic,Normative,Causal,Statistical,Constraint,Heuristic,Procedural\}
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a nine-member rule-kind taxonomy: Logical, Mathematical, Semantic, Normative, Causal, Statistical, Constraint, Heuristic, Procedural.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Logical rules ... A, A\Rightarrow B therefore B. This is ModusPonens. Its validity depends on the logical system. ... Mathematical rules ... \Gamma\vdash_{\mathcal M} P ... x=2 and y=x+3 imply y=5. This is not merely a business rule. It has formal mathematical semantics.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Logical rules (Modus Ponens, valid relative to a logical system) and Mathematical rules (Γ⊢_M P, worked with an arithmetic example) as having formal semantics distinct from business rules.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Semantic rules ... Dog\subseteq Animal and Rex\in Dog. Then Rex\in Animal. This is SemanticInference. It depends on \mathcal O. K,\mathcal O\vdash Rex\in Animal. ... Normative rules ... Production changes require approval. ProductionChange(x)\Rightarrow RequiresApproval(x). This is not a statement a
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Semantic rules (ontology-relative inference, K,O⊢P) and Normative rules (what must be done, not what is true) — NormativeRule ≠ DescriptiveRule, essential for Governance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Constraint rules ... ProductionService\Rightarrow HasOwner. A state violating this condition is InvalidState. A constraint does not necessarily tell us what caused the violation. It tells us: The current state does not satisfy the required condition. ... Causal rules ... do(FirewallChange)\rightarro
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Constraint rules (admissible-state conditions, silent on cause) and Causal rules (requiring a causal model) — CausalRule ≠ LogicalRule, since a causal relation cannot simply feed a logical theorem prover.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Statistical rules ... P(Failure\mid ConfigurationA)=0.8 while P(Failure\mid ConfigurationB)=0.1. That is statistical evidence. It does not automatically produce ConfigurationA\Rightarrow Failure. Probability\neq Logical Implication. This is one of the most important safeguards against bad AI reasoni
b_rows_sample.statement: States Probability ≠ Logical Implication as one of the most important safeguards against bad AI reasoning, illustrated by conditional failure probabilities not implying a deterministic rule.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Heuristic rules ... If CPU usage is high and latency increases, investigate resource saturation. This is useful. But it is not necessarily logically valid. Heuristic inference produces candidates, not guaranteed conclusions. Its epistemic status must remain visible. ... Procedural rules ... To deplo
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Heuristic rules (producing candidates, not guaranteed conclusions) and Procedural rules (operational how-to, not logical inference) — Procedure ≠ Inference.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The inference operation ... I:(K,R)\rightarrow C ... Rule is the specification; Inference is the application. ... An inference record ... J=(InferenceID,Premises,Rule,Conclusion,Context,Model,Timestamp,Provenance). This gives us an auditable derivation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Separates Rule (specification) from Inference I:(K,R)→C (application), requiring an auditable InferenceRecord J=(InferenceID,Premises,Rule,Conclusion,Context,Model,Timestamp,Provenance).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Derived knowledge ... SourceAssertion from DerivedAssertion. The derived assertion has provenance DerivedFrom(J). DerivedKnowledge\neq DirectObservation. ... Epistemic state of derived knowledge ... \Sigma_{derived} must not automatically inherit \Sigma_{source}. Support(DerivedConclusion) depends o
b_rows_sample.statement: States DerivedKnowledge ≠ DirectObservation and that a derived assertion's epistemic state must not automatically inherit its source's — Support(DerivedConclusion) depends on both Support(Premises) and Trustworthiness(ApplicableRule).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Rule applicability ... ProductionChange\Rightarrow RequiresApproval. If Change=DevelopmentChange, then R does not apply. Applicable(R,K,Ctx,t) before inference. ... Context is part of inference ... Inference = f(K,R,Context,Time,Policy). Not simply f(K,R). This connects directly to our Step 17 seman
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines an Applicable(R,K,Ctx,t) precondition gating rule use, and generalizes inference to Inference=f(K,R,Context,Time,Policy), not merely f(K,R).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Rule precedence ... R_1: ProductionChange\Rightarrow RequiresApproval. R_2: EmergencyChange\Rightarrow ImmediateExecution. We need explicit precedence or conflict-resolution policy. KnowledgeOS must not invent one. ... Rule conflict ... RuleConflict(R_1,R_2,Ctx,t) with status Detected \rightarrow In
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires explicit precedence/conflict-resolution policy when rules conflict (RuleConflict(R1,R2,Ctx,t), status lifecycle Detected→Investigated→Resolved/Unresolvable), warning KnowledgeOS must never invent one; states Priority ≠ Truth — rule precedence is a governance choice, not greater correctness.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Rules can be conditional ... A\land B\land C\Rightarrow D. KnowledgeOS must determine whether A,B,C are true; false; unknown. Eval(P,K)\in\{True,False,Unknown\}. ... Unknown premises ... A=True, B=Unknown, A\land B\Rightarrow C. We cannot conclude C=True. Unknown premise does not become True. This i
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines three-valued rule evaluation Eval(P,K)∈{T,F,U} with Kleene-style conjunction/disjunction tables (T∧U=U, F∧U=F, T∨U=T, F∨U=U), so an unknown premise never becomes True by default.

b_rows_sample.anchor: But three-valued logic is not enough everywhere ... four-valued logic; paraconsistent logic; probabilistic reasoning; temporal logic; modal logic; fuzzy logic; default reasoning. KnowledgeOS should not mandate one universal logic. Instead it needs a reasoning framework capable of hosting multiple in
b_rows_sample.statement: Lists seven logic families beyond three-valued logic (four-valued, paraconsistent, probabilistic, temporal, modal, fuzzy, default) that KnowledgeOS should not be forced to choose among — it needs a framework hosting multiple inference semantics.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Paraconsistent reasoning ... Nexus=3.69 and Nexus=3.72 ... Both may be present because their temporal/contextual scopes differ or because the system genuinely has contradictory information. We should not allow A\land\neg A to cause arbitrary conclusions. ... KnowledgeOS should support contradiction-
b_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms KnowledgeOS's paraconsistent stance (contradiction is a state to manage, not a failure) and distinguishes Unknown(A) from Conflict(A,¬A) — Unknown ≠ Conflict.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Inference closure ... Cl_R(K) ... K_0=K, K_{i+1}=K_i\cup Infer(K_i,R). When K_{i+1}=K_i, we reach a fixed point K^*=Cl_R(K). This is computationally useful. ... But not all reasoning is monotonic ... KnowledgeOS absolutely needs non-monotonic behavior. We believe the server is healthy. Later: New mo
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines an inference closure fixpoint Cl_R(K) for finite monotonic rule sets, then argues KnowledgeOS is fundamentally non-monotonic, requiring a defeasible entailment ⊢_def distinct from ordinary ⊢, where a defeasible conclusion may later cease to hold.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Example ... Normally HealthyHost\Rightarrow AvailableService. KnowledgeOS derives AvailableService. Then a new fact appears MaintenanceWindow. The previous conclusion may no longer hold. NewKnowledge can invalidate previous derived knowledge. This connects directly to our temporal and revision model
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked non-monotonic example: a default health→availability inference is invalidated by a later-discovered maintenance window, connecting to the temporal and revision model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Rule provenance ... Rule: ProductionChangeRequiresApproval ... Source: IT Change Management Framework v0.9 ... Authority: Architecture Governance ... Effective: 2026-06-01 ... Version: 0.9. That makes the inference auditable. ... LLM-generated rules ... If certificate expiry is within 30 days, recom
b_rows_sample.statement: Requires full rule provenance (Source, Authority, Effective date, Version) for auditability, and mandates LLM-proposed rules enter only as CandidateRule, never automatically becoming GovernedRule — LLMGeneratedRule ≠ AuthorizedRule.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Rule lifecycle ... Candidate → Reviewed → Validated → Approved → Active → Superseded → Retired. This is analogous to the lifecycle we already defined for assertions and decisions. ... Rule versioning ... If R_1 is replaced by R_2, historical conclusions based on R_1 must remain traceable. DerivedKno
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a seven-stage rule lifecycle (Candidate→Reviewed→Validated→Approved→Active→Superseded→Retired) and requires derived knowledge reference RuleVersion, with full reproducibility requiring Premises+RuleVersion+SemanticModelVersion+PolicyVersion+Context+TemporalScope.

Note: S0875's Step 18: Rule!=Inference!=Truth!=Policy; nine rule Kinds with worked non-equivalences (Logical/Mathematical/Semantic/Normative/Causal/Statistical/Constraint/Heuristic/Procedural); Rule-as-specification vs Inference-as-application; three-valued rule evaluation; non-monotonic revision; a ReasoningEngine=Orchestrator+SpecializedReasoners architecture with a compiler analogy; Proof!=Explanation; four reasoning-result states; R1-R14 invariants; hands off to Step 19 (authority/trust/evidence-weighting/source-reliability/knowledge-commitment).

a_rows_sample.anchor: A set of sentences D_{S_\alpha} is a progression of the initial database D_{S_0} to S_\alpha iff ... Progression is not always first-order definable. Finite progression is second-order definable. ... STRIPS Operator: Precondition P, Delete list D, Add list A ... Correctness Theorem: For suitable basic action theories, the STRIPS plan is equivalent to the situation calculus plan.
a_rows_sample.statement: Formal progression definition (S_alpha-uniform sentences whose models each correspond to an original-theory model with identical future behavior), with the limitation that progression is not always first-order definable (finite progression is second-order definable); STRIPS (precondition/delete-list/add-list operators, remove-then-add successor database) formalized as a restricted case of progression, with a correctness theorem equating STRIPS plans to situation-calculus plans for suitable basic action theories.

b_rows_sample.anchor: R[W] reducing a query about a later situation to a query about the initial situation ... Eval_c \neq ReasoningAlgorithm ... Reason_S(K,r) \rightarrow EvidenceForEvaluation rather than claiming Regression = Eval
b_rows_sample.statement: Regression R[W] is offered as a candidate reasoning mechanism feeding Eval_c, explicitly distinguished as Eval_c != ReasoningAlgorithm: Reason_S(K,r) -> EvidenceForEvaluation, rejecting the identification Regression = Eval.

b_rows_sample.anchor: R[F(x,do(a,s))] = R[Phi_F(x,a,s)] ... The Regression Theorem: D \models W \iff D_{S_0}\cup D_{una}\models R[W] ... Progression is harder than regression—it may not be first-order definable.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the formal Regression Theorem (D |= W iff D_S0 ∪ D_una |= R[W], reducing entailment over the full domain axiomatization to entailment over the initial-situation axioms plus unique-names axioms via regression R), and notes progression may not be first-order definable, making it strictly harder than regression -- both retained as [DERIVED] legitimate reasoning mechanisms.

b_rows_sample.statement: Executed equivalence check: for 6 action sequences (including empty, single, and multi-fluent-affecting sequences) crossed with 2 fluents, backward regression and forward progression agree on all 12 resulting truth values, confirming the regression theorem holds in this toy basic action theory.

b_rows_sample.anchor: class Situation: """A situation IS a history: a finite sequence of actions.  NOT a state.""" ... def successor(self, a, state): """Successor state axiom:  F' = gamma+ ∨ (F ∧ ¬gamma-)""" ... def regress(self, fluent, sit): """REGRESSION: rewrite a query about sit into a query about S0, by unwinding the successor-state axiom backwards."""
b_rows_sample.statement: A minimal but faithful executable model of Reiter's situation calculus: a Situation as an immutable action tuple (explicitly a history, not a state), an ActionTheory with Poss/successor(SSA)/progress/executable/regress methods, used to generate all five A1-A5 experimental results in this batch; module docstring explicitly frames these as verification tests of Reiter's machinery, not a KnowledgeOS implementation, and states nothing here promotes any Reiter concept to a KnowledgeOS primitive.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Regression and progression agree on 12/12 checks across 6 action sequences x 2 fluents (A3). Executed, not asserted. ... Progression computes A_{t+1} and discards the history. KR-HISTORY established that the kernel writes history (and reads it 0 times). Progression satisfies the read behaviour and not the write obligation. ... progression for the state, history retained for audit, regression as the mechanism that makes retention useful rather than merely dutiful.
b_rows_sample.statement: New synthesis: regression and progression serve complementary, not competing, roles for KnowledgeOS -- progression advances the state (satisfying the kernel's 0-read behavior) while history must still be retained to satisfy a separate write obligation established by KR-HISTORY, and regression is what makes that retained history useful for audit/verification rather than merely dutiful storage; P10 (progression sufficient alone) is refuted on exactly this basis. The regression theorem's formal guarantee is unavailable to KnowledgeOS (no basic action theory exists yet) -- only the mechanism's shape transfers.

b_rows_sample.statement: IC-2: regression (R[phi] unwinding the successor-state axioms to S0) is proposed as a verification mechanism, motivated by the corpus finding (KR-HISTORY) that history is written and never read -- regression is what would make it readable for audit. Terminates on regressable queries, deterministic, and A3 confirms regression agrees with progression 12/12. But KnowledgeOS has no basic action theory, so the regression theorem's formal guarantee is unavailable -- only the mechanism's shape transfers. Status: SUPPORTED as the most transferable item, yet still not adoptable.

a_rows_sample.statement: EXP-19: tested against 10 propositions the corpus itself states it needs to express, P=(Entity,Dimension,Value) cleanly expresses only 2; 3 are inexpressible (negation — no negative values in V_D; conditional — 'IF v>=3.60 THEN patch-current', the founding conditional-determination problem; universal quantification — 'every committee has >=3 members'); 2 are lossy (a validity interval collapses to one timestamp t; a unit is dropped); 1 ('A1 contradicts A2') is not a proposition at all in this type system and must be expressed as an R-edge instead, giving the theory two uncoordinated mechanisms for propositional content; 1 ('Nexus is ready to migrate') is expressible but empty, holding the conclusion with no way to express the rule that produced it; 1 ('Nexus.version is UNKNOWN') is ambiguous between a value-space category error and true absence.

b_rows_sample.statement: Quotes Q7's original three-level type chain verbatim: Proposition P=(E,D,V) (content only), Assertion A=(P,Sigma,E,tau,Pi) (proposition embedded plus epistemic state Sigma, evidence E, temporal validity tau, provenance Pi), Knowledge State K_t=(A_t,R_t,E_t,H_t,Z_t,L_t) (a collection of assertions plus further components); Q7 itself names collapsing P, A and K_t as the single biggest mathematical problem in the document and explicitly refuses to accept an equation collapsing them.

b_rows_sample.statement: Instead of treating delta as an unspecified transformer, investigate K_{t+1}=Succ(K_t,e_t) where each state component carries conditions for becoming true, becoming false, and persistence — i.e. the frame problem, borrowed from situation-calculus successor-state axioms F(x,do(a,s)) ≡ gamma_F(x,a,s) v (F(x,s) & ¬delta_F(x,a,s)).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Table: what I would actually add to KnowledgeOS Theory v1.3 (T1-T5) vs What I would NOT adopt
b_rows_sample.statement: Recorded editorial recommendation: five candidate theoretical commitments (T1 explicit/implicit knowledge, T2 reasoning is semantics-dependent Cn_S(K), T3 evaluation may consume implicit knowledge Eval_c(Cn_S(K),r,Gamma), T4 state transition needs persistence semantics Succ_S, T5 explanation is not determination) proposed for Theory v1.3 as strong candidates, none yet kernel-promoted; explicitly rejects Sat=FOL-entailment, Zero=CWA, Zero=Delta=empty universally, Boundary=frame axioms, delta=situation calculus, Identity=unique-names+domain-closure, DL=Boundary-taxonomy, mandatory default reasoning, FOL-as-representation-language, and YES/NO/UNKNOWN-sufficiency.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t+1}=Succ_{\mathcal S}(K_t,e_t) ... successor semantics must account for: newly introduced content; removed or invalidated content; persistent content; contextual applicability; provenance/history. This does not define δ as situation calculus.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A representation is adequate for a question only if the distinctions required to answer that question are preserved by the representation. a_rows_sample.statement: States the candidate [PROP] Representation Adequacy Principle: Adequate(pi,Q) implies D_Q subseteq Preserved(pi), i.e. a representation is adequate for a question only if it preserves the distinctions that question requires -- explicitly a research hypothesis, not yet an established law, and judged potentially more fundamental than the individual Sat/Gap/Zero proposals.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I attacked my own proposal. Ten attacks, executed. 7 survived, 3 refuted.
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs 10 executed adversarial attacks against the candidate knowledge-state tuple K={(q,s,e,c,t,u)}; 7 survive: expressing Unknown (s=Unknown,e=empty,u=unknown, distinct from Refuted), expressing contradiction as a computable relation over two items (not a state property), distinguishing missingness-from-K from present-with-Unknown, provenance without circularity (evidence field e holds opaque evidence-reference ids, not evidence objects, so K need not contain E and E need not contain K), a base case K0 with zero transformations existing (breaking the assumed K->T->K cycle dependency), decidable structural equality (frozenset of frozen records), and supersession via closing t.valid_to plus adding a successor (no extra field needed, bitemporality suffices).

a_rows_sample.anchor: R1 -- non-identifiability is NOT a field... R2 -- structural equality is insufficient... R3 -- the status type is mine, not the corpus's.
a_rows_sample.statement: Three of the ten attacks refute the original proposal: R1, non-identifiability must be a relation over (K1,K2,H,Q) -- two states observationally equivalent under an observation map -- not a label-valued attribute of one item; R2, structural equality is insufficient, shown by an executed counterexample where identical knowledge re-ingested under a new evidence id (E-001 -> E-001-dup) is structurally unequal, so equality must be a FAMILY of relations, not one; R3, the STATUS_VOCAB type is the verifier's own invention -- the corpus has eleven competing vocabularies and designates none, so status is UNDERDETERMINED BY CORPUS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Item = (q: Prop, s: Status, e: FrozenSet[EvidenceRef], c: Context, t: Interval(...), u: Unc) ... eq_struct, eq_sem, eq_obs ... nonidentifiable(K1,K2,H,Q) ... G(input,K,ctx,auth,pol) in {0,1}
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a repaired, fully executable knowledge-state kernel: Item=(q,s,e,c,t,u) with K=FrozenSet[Item]; an equality FAMILY of three distinct relations (eq_struct: literal equality; eq_sem: equality ignoring evidence ids/uncertainty width; eq_obs: equality relative to an explicit observation map H); non-identifiability as the relation H(K1)=H(K2) AND Q(K1)!=Q(K2); and a total, decidable governance predicate G(input,K,ctx,auth,pol) in {0,1}. Every symbol has an explicit value -- no placeholders or oracles.
